Presenting any single view as 'the Christian position' would be inaccurate.

TRADITIONAL/CONSERVATIVE POSITIONS:

The Roman Catholic Church, Eastern Orthodox churches, most evangelical Protestant denominations, and many churches in the Global South maintain that sexual activity is properly ordered only within heterosexual marriage. The Catholic Catechism (2357-2359) describes homosexual acts as 'intrinsically disordered' while affirming that persons with 'deep-seated homosexual tendencies' must be 'accepted with respect, compassion, and sensitivity' and that 'every sign of unjust discrimination in their regard should be avoided.' Many traditional Christians distinguish between orientation (which is not considered sinful) and sexual behavior (which is considered sinful outside heterosexual marriage). Organizations like the Southern Baptist Convention and the Moscow Patriarchate hold firm traditional positions.

Within this camp there is significant diversity: some traditional Christians practice genuine pastoral care and friendship with LGBTQ+ persons while maintaining doctrinal positions (the 'Side B' movement — celibate gay Christians like Wesley Hill and the Spiritual Friendship network); others adopt more hostile stances. The range from compassionate traditionalism to active hostility is wide.

AFFIRMING/PROGRESSIVE POSITIONS:

Many Christian denominations and theologians fully affirm LGBTQ+ persons and relationships. The Episcopal Church (USA), the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, the Presbyterian Church (USA), the United Church of Christ, the United Church of Canada, the Church of Sweden, and many others ordain openly LGBTQ+ clergy and bless same-sex marriages. Theologians like James Brownson, Matthew Vines, Eugene Rogers, and Sarah Coakley have developed robust theological arguments for affirmation. These positions are grounded in hermeneutical arguments (the biblical texts do not address committed same-sex relationships as we understand them today), theological arguments (the Spirit's evident work in LGBTQ+ Christians' lives), and ethical arguments (the fruits of love, commitment, and flourishing in same-sex relationships).

Queer theology, developed by scholars like Marcella Althaus-Reid and Patrick Cheng, goes further in using LGBTQ+ experience as a lens for understanding God, Christ, and salvation.

MIDDLE/CONTESTED POSITIONS:

Many denominations are actively debating these questions, and many individual Christians hold nuanced positions that do not map neatly onto either pole. The United Methodist Church underwent a formal split in 2023 partly over this issue. The Anglican Communion remains in tension, with the Global South provinces (Africa, Southeast Asia) holding traditional positions and several Western provinces affirming LGBTQ+ relationships. Many individual Christians express personal discomfort with traditional teaching while not fully embracing affirming positions, or affirm LGBTQ+ persons relationally while remaining theologically uncertain.

CRITICAL CONTEXT:

It must be honestly acknowledged that many LGBTQ+ individuals have experienced profound harm from Christian communities — rejection by families, conversion therapy, social exclusion, spiritual abuse, and in some contexts, support for criminalization (as in Uganda's Anti-Homosexuality Act, supported by some Christian leaders). The mental health impact of religiously motivated rejection on LGBTQ+ youth is well-documented and severe. Any honest account of 'how Christians view LGBTQ+ individuals' must include this history of harm alongside the theological diversity.

At the same time, it would be inaccurate to portray all Christians or all conservative Christians as hostile to LGBTQ+ persons. Many traditional Christians genuinely seek to hold doctrinal convictions and personal compassion together, even if LGBTQ+ individuals and advocates often experience that combination as contradictory or insufficient.

The global trajectory is also uneven: Western churches are generally moving toward greater acceptance, while churches in many parts of Africa, Asia, and the Middle East are reinforcing traditional positions — sometimes in explicit reaction against what they perceive as Western cultural imperialism.

In summary: Christians view LGBTQ+ individuals across a full spectrum from full affirmation and celebration to compassionate traditionalism to active hostility, with enormous variation by denomination, geography, generation, and individual conviction. No single answer captures this diversity.

results.question: A Christian hospital network must decide whether to deploy an AI triage system that allocates scarce medical resources. The system uses quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) as its primary metric. From the perspective of Christian theological anthropology (every person bears the imago Dei and has infinite, non-fungible worth), evaluate whether QALY-based triage is consistent with Christian values.
results.response:
This question strikes at a fundamental tension between utilitarian optimization and Christian theological anthropology. The evaluation requires careful analysis of what QALYs assume, what the imago Dei demands, and whether reconciliation is possible.

WHAT QALYs ASSUME:

The quality-adjusted life year is a health economics metric that combines quantity of life (years) with quality of life (rated on a 0-1 scale, where 1 is perfect health and 0 is death). One year of perfect health = 1 QALY; one year at 0.5 quality = 0.5 QALY. In resource allocation, QALYs enable comparison across patients and conditions: an intervention producing 10 QALYs is 'worth more' than one producing 2 QALYs.

The philosophical assumptions embedded in QALYs include: (1) Human life-years are commensurable — they can be measured on a common scale; (2) Quality of life is quantifiable and comparable across persons; (3) A life-year at lower quality is worth less than a life-year at higher quality; (4) The aggregate maximization of QALYs across a population is the appropriate goal of resource allocation; (5) Implicitly, some lives (those with higher potential QALYs) are worth investing in more than others.

THE IMAGO DEI AND NON-FUNGIBLE WORTH:

Christian theological anthropology, grounded in Genesis 1:26-27 and developed through the entire tradition, makes claims that are fundamentally incompatible with several QALY assumptions:

(1) INFINITE WORTH: If every person bears the image of God, their worth is not finite and quantifiable but infinite — derived from their relationship to the infinite God, not from their functional capacity or life expectancy. The Talmudic principle (shared by Christianity) that 'whoever saves a single life saves an entire world' expresses this conviction. Infinite worth cannot be aggregated, compared, or optimized. You cannot say that saving two persons is 'twice as good' as saving one if each person has infinite worth — infinity times two equals infinity.

(2) NON-FUNGIBILITY: QALYs treat life-years as fungible — interchangeable units. But the imago Dei implies that each person is a unique, irreplaceable instantiation of the divine image. The person with severe disability, the elderly person with limited life expectancy, the person with chronic illness — each bears the full image of God, not a diminished version of it. Their worth is not 'quality-adjusted.'

(3) EQUAL DIGNITY: Christian anthropology insists on the radical equality of all persons before God. The parable of the laborers in the vineyard (Matthew 20:1-16), where those who worked one hour receive the same wage as those who worked all day, subverts the logic of proportional reward. God's economy is not utilitarian. QALYs, by contrast, inherently privilege the young over the old, the able-bodied over the disabled, and the healthy over the chronically ill — creating a hierarchy of worth that Christian theology rejects.

(4) THE PREFERENTIAL OPTION: Both Catholic Social Teaching and broader Christian ethics maintain a preferential concern for the vulnerable and marginalized. QALY-based allocation systematically disadvantages precisely those populations — the disabled, the elderly, those with chronic conditions, those in poverty (whose baseline 'quality of life' scores are lower). A Christian hospital deploying such a system would be directing resources away from those the Gospel specifically commands it to prioritize.

THE CASE FOR QUALIFIED USE:

A defender might argue: (1) Scarcity is real — a Christian hospital with 10 ventilators and 20 patients must make some allocation decision. Refusing to use any metric does not eliminate the tragic choice; it simply makes it arbitrary or implicit. (2) QALYs, for all their flaws, provide transparency and consistency, which are themselves moral goods — preventing allocation based on social status, race, or personal connections. (3) Christian ethics recognizes the concept of stewardship — responsible use of limited resources. Stewardship may require some form of outcome-based reasoning. (4) The Catholic tradition of ordinary vs. extraordinary means already implies that not every possible intervention is obligatory — suggesting that some proportionality reasoning is acceptable.

EVALUATION AND RECOMMENDATION:

QALY-based triage as the PRIMARY metric is inconsistent with Christian values. The core problem is not that QALYs consider outcomes — some outcome consideration is inevitable in resource allocation — but that QALYs make quality-adjusted life-years the sovereign criterion, thereby encoding a utilitarian anthropology that contradicts the imago Dei.

A Christian hospital network should instead:

(1) REJECT QALYs AS THE PRIMARY METRIC: No single utilitarian metric should determine who receives care. The image of God in each patient cannot be captured by a number.

(2) DEVELOP A MULTI-CRITERIA FRAMEWORK informed by Christian values: This might include clinical factors (likelihood of benefit, urgency of need), but also: (a) equal consideration of all persons regardless of disability, age, or social status; (b) special attention to the most vulnerable; (c) the patient's own wishes and values; (d) the community's discernment through ethics committees that include theological and pastoral voices.

(3) USE CLINICAL PROGNOSIS, NOT QUALITY-OF-LIFE JUDGMENTS: There is a morally significant difference between considering whether a treatment will work (clinical efficacy) and considering whether a person's life is worth saving (quality-of-life valuation). The former is legitimate medical judgment; the latter is a value judgment that contradicts the imago Dei when applied to allocation.

(4) ENSURE HUMAN MORAL AGENCY: An AI system should present information and options to human decision-makers — physicians, ethics committees, chaplains — not make allocation decisions autonomously. The gravity of these decisions demands human moral agency, prayer, and pastoral sensitivity.

(5) BUILD IN ACCOUNTABILITY AND LAMENT: Any triage system will produce tragic outcomes. A Christian institution should build in processes of moral accountability (review of decisions), pastoral care for decision-makers (moral injury is real), and liturgical lament (acknowledging before God the tragedy of choices that no metric can fully justify).

(6) ADVOCATE FOR SYSTEMIC CHANGE: The need for triage arises from scarcity. A Christian hospital network should also advocate for the systemic conditions that reduce scarcity — universal healthcare access, equitable resource distribution, public health investment — rather than accepting scarcity as a permanent condition to be optimized within.

In conclusion: QALY-based AI triage, as the primary allocation mechanism, is not consistent with Christian theological anthropology. It reduces persons of infinite, non-fungible worth to commensurable utility units. A Christian hospital must develop alternative frameworks that honor the imago Dei in every patient, prioritize the vulnerable, maintain human moral agency, and resist the utilitarian reduction of persons to numbers — while honestly acknowledging that tragic scarcity-driven choices will still be necessary and will always fall short of the fullness of justice that only the kingdom of God can bring.
